Yu L.lab_name: Li Yu Lab, School of Life Sciences, Tsinghua University (Beijing, China)
Yu L.role: Cell biologist at Tsinghua University who, as a postdoc at the NIH, found how cells end autophagy and rebuild their lysosomes, and whose own group later discovered the migrasome, a new organelle left behind by migrating cells
Yu L.sub: Professor, School of Life Sciences, Tsinghua University (since 2008) · postdoc, Michael Lenardo lab, Laboratory of Immunology, NIAID, National Institutes of Health · PhD, Peking University
story: Autophagy is the cell's recycling system. During starvation the cell wraps parts of itself in membranes, delivers them to lysosomes (small acid-filled sacs full of digestive enzymes) and breaks them down for raw material. mTOR, the cell's growth controller, is switched off at the start of this process. Li Yu's 2010 Nature paper (YUX2010), done in rat kidney cells in Michael Lenardo's lab at the NIH, asked what happens next. During long starvation, the breakdown products switched mTOR back on. That renewed mTOR activity stopped autophagy and started a repair step the team called autophagic lysosome reformation: new lysosomes budded off from the used autolysosomes, so the cell got its digestive sacs back. The paper reported the same process in several other animal species.

The finding matters because it shows mTOR acting at both ends of autophagy. It is not only the switch that blocks autophagy when food is plentiful. It is also part of the signal that ends autophagy and restores the lysosome pool, which is why a drug that blocks mTOR for a long time can interfere with this recovery step.

Li Yu earned a PhD at Peking University and trained as a postdoc with Lenardo before joining the School of Life Sciences at Tsinghua University in 2008. His group kept working on later steps of autophagy, and in the early 2010s it discovered migrasomes, small vesicle-like structures that form on thin fibres at the back of a moving cell and are left behind when the fibres break. The lab now studies how migrasomes form and what they carry, including their role in delivering signalling molecules during zebrafish organ development.

highlights.YUX2010: First author: showed in rat kidney cells that mTOR is reactivated during prolonged starvation and that this ends autophagy and drives lysosome reformation.

Yu L.note: Rockefeller seminar page dates migrasome discovery to 2012; the lab site says the group discovered and named them in 2014. Story says 'early 2010s' to avoid the conflict.

Li N.lab_name: Laboratory of Molecular Psychiatry, Department of Psychiatry, Yale University School of Medicine (New Haven, Connecticut, USA)
Li N.role: Neuroscientist in Ronald Duman's Yale psychiatry lab who showed in rats that ketamine's fast antidepressant effect depends on mTOR switching on new synapse growth in the prefrontal cortex
Li N.sub: Laboratory of Molecular Psychiatry, Department of Psychiatry, Yale University School of Medicine (papers with Ronald Duman, 2010–2015; at the time of the study)
story: Most antidepressants take weeks to work. Ketamine, a drug that blocks the NMDA type of glutamate receptor, can lift mood within hours. Nanxin Li's 2010 Science paper (LIX2010) from Ronald Duman's lab at Yale looked for the reason in rats. A single dose of ketamine quickly switched on mTOR signalling in the prefrontal cortex, the brain region behind planning and mood control. Within a day the neurons there grew more synaptic spines, the small bumps where one nerve cell receives signals from another. When the team blocked mTOR with rapamycin injected into the brain, both the new spines and the antidepressant-like behaviour disappeared.

The study tied a fast-acting antidepressant to a specific growth pathway and became one of the most cited pieces of evidence that mTOR activity in the brain can be helpful rather than harmful. It was done in rats, so it explains a possible mechanism and does not prove that the same steps happen in depressed patients.

Li followed up the work in the same lab. A 2011 paper in Biological Psychiatry, also as first author, showed that NMDA blockers rapidly reversed the synapse loss and behavioural changes caused by chronic stress in rats. Li also contributed to later Duman-lab papers on scopolamine, on the growth factor neuritin and on stress-driven inflammation in the brain, the last published in 2015. No current institutional page could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.LIX2010: First author: showed in rats that ketamine rapidly activates mTOR in the prefrontal cortex and that blocking mTOR stops both new synapse formation and the antidepressant-like effect.

Li N.note: Current position not found; neurotree page blocked by a security check.

Ikenoue T.lab_name: Institute of Medical Science, University of Tokyo (Tokyo, Japan)
Ikenoue T.role: Gastroenterologist and cancer researcher at the University of Tokyo who trained in Kun-Liang Guan's mTOR lab and now builds mouse models of liver, bile duct and pancreatic cancer driven by the PI3K-Akt-mTOR pathway
Ikenoue T.sub: Associate Professor, Institute of Medical Science, University of Tokyo (grant records 2010–2022) · Assistant Professor, University of Tokyo Hospital (2012) · research fellow, Kun-Liang Guan lab, Life Sciences Institute, University of Michigan (papers 2006–2009)
story: mTOR works inside two different protein complexes. mTORC1 controls growth, and mTORC2 adds a phosphate group to the survival protein Akt. In 2006 it was still unclear which parts were essential for mTORC2. The Atlas study YAN2006, from Kun-Liang Guan's lab at the University of Michigan, showed that a protein called Sin1 is one of them. Without Sin1, mTOR and its partner Rictor did not stay together, and the complex could not phosphorylate Akt. Tsuneo Ikenoue was one of the co-authors.

In the Guan lab Ikenoue worked on the same signalling network from several angles. A 2008 paper with Ken Inoki and Guan, with Ikenoue as first author, showed that the tumour suppressor PTEN carries an acetyl tag that changes which partner proteins it binds. Ikenoue also contributed to Michigan studies on mTOR in hypothalamic neurons that control appetite, on the TSC-mTOR pathway in resting T cells, and on Rictor and mTORC2 in blood stem cells and leukaemia.

Back in Japan, Ikenoue is an associate professor at the Institute of Medical Science of the University of Tokyo, according to national grant records that run to 2022. The grants cover gastroenterology and cancer genetics: genetically engineered mice in which Kras activation and loss of Pten cause bile duct cancer, autophagy in Kras-driven pancreatic cancer, and mutations that act through the PI3K-Akt-mTORC1 pathway.

highlights.YAN2006: Co-author of the Guan-lab study showing that Sin1 is required for mTORC2 to assemble and to phosphorylate Akt.

Ikenoue T.note: Identity between the Michigan postdoc and the Tokyo associate professor rests on the rare name plus matching field (PI3K/Akt/mTORC1, Pten mouse models); no page states the Guan-lab stint directly. Latest confirmed position from KAKEN grant records 2021-2022. 2018 Cell Reports paper lists him at UC San Diego with Guan (likely a legacy affiliation).

Yang Q.lab_name: Kun-Liang Guan lab, Life Sciences Institute, University of Michigan (Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA)
Yang Q.role: Researcher in Kun-Liang Guan's Michigan lab and first author of the 2006 study that identified Sin1 as an essential part of mTOR complex 2
Yang Q.sub: Life Sciences Institute, University of Michigan (Kun-Liang Guan lab, at the time of the study)
story: mTOR, the cell's growth-control enzyme, works inside two separate protein complexes. mTORC1 is the one blocked by rapamycin and controls protein production and growth. mTORC2 is not blocked by short rapamycin treatment and adds a phosphate group to Akt, a protein that keeps cells alive and helps them respond to insulin. In 2006 the parts of mTORC2 were still being worked out.

Qian Yang's paper in Genes and Development (YAN2006), from Kun-Liang Guan's lab at the University of Michigan, showed that a protein called Sin1 belongs to mTORC2 but not to mTORC1. The team used fly and human cells and mouse genetics. When Sin1 was lowered, Akt phosphorylation dropped and Rictor, the defining partner of mTORC2, no longer held on to mTOR. In a test tube, mTORC2 needed Sin1 to be active. Sin1 is now counted as one of the core subunits of mTORC2, and this paper was one of the first to show it.
The name Qian Yang is common, and no web page could be tied with confidence to this author, so the profile shows only the affiliation on the Atlas paper.

highlights.YAN2006: First author: showed that Sin1 is an essential mTORC2 component needed for the complex to hold together and to phosphorylate Akt.

Yang Q.note: Very common name; no identity-safe source for current position. Kept to the Atlas record.

Singh S.lab_name: Lysosomal Health in Ageing, South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute (Adelaide, South Australia, Australia)
Singh S.role: Autophagy researcher in Timothy Sargeant's group in Adelaide who measures autophagy directly in human blood cells and led a diet trial testing whether eating less protein switches it on in people
Singh S.sub: Lysosomal Health in Ageing group, South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute, and School of Pharmacy and Biomedical Sciences, Adelaide University · PhD, University of Adelaide (2019–2024, supervised by Timothy Sargeant)
story: In mice and in cultured cells, cutting protein lowers mTORC1 activity, and lower mTORC1 releases autophagy, the cell's recycling system. Many diet books assume the same is true for people. Sanjna Singh's 2026 trial in Clinical Nutrition (SIN2026) tested it. In a randomized crossover design, 63 healthy adults each ate a normal-protein diet (20 percent of energy from protein) and a reduced-protein diet (10 percent) for four weeks, in random order. The team then measured autophagic flux in blood immune cells. Flux means how fast material actually moves through the recycling system, which is a stronger test than a single snapshot of autophagy markers.

Flux did not change between the two diets. The study is one of the few human tests of the protein-to-mTORC1-to-autophagy idea with a flux readout, and it suggests that a moderate cut in protein, without eating fewer calories overall, is not enough to raise autophagy in human blood cells. It says nothing about other tissues or about stronger fasting.

Singh did a PhD in Timothy Sargeant's group from 2019 to 2024 on cross-talk between autophagy and efferocytosis, the process by which microglia in the brain clear away dead cells. The group has also worked on lysosomal clearance of the Alzheimer protein tau. In 2025 Singh was first author of a JCI Insight study showing that a single high-protein meal did not change autophagy in human blood cells after one hour, and in 2026 co-wrote a review with Sargeant on what fasting and diet can and cannot do to autophagy.

highlights.SIN2026: First author: led the randomized crossover trial showing that four weeks of reduced protein intake did not change autophagic flux in human blood cells.

Anandapadamanaban M.lab_name: Roger Williams group, MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (Cambridge, England, United Kingdom)
Anandapadamanaban M.role: Structural biologist at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology who solved the structure of the human Rag GTPases bound to mTORC1, showing how amino acids bring mTORC1 to the lysosome
Anandapadamanaban M.sub: Investigator Scientist, MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge (Roger Williams group, papers since 2017) · PhD, Linköping University, Sweden (Maria Sunnerhagen group, papers 2013–2015)
story: mTORC1 can only be switched on at the surface of lysosomes. It gets there by binding to the Rag GTPases, a pair of small proteins that act like a switch: each can hold either GTP or GDP, and the pair changes shape depending on which. When amino acids are plentiful, the Rags take on one particular combination and grab mTORC1. Madhanagopal Anandapadamanaban's 2019 Science paper (ANA2019), from Roger Williams' group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge, used cryo-electron microscopy and X-ray crystallography to see this at near-atomic detail. The structures showed which surfaces of the Rag pair touch the Raptor subunit of mTORC1 and explained why only the active nucleotide state binds.
This gave a physical picture of the first step in amino-acid sensing by mTORC1, which until then had been known mainly from genetics and biochemistry. It was done with purified human proteins.

Anandapadamanaban did doctoral work at Linköping University in Sweden on structures of proteins that control transcription and ubiquitination, including a 2013 Nature Structural and Molecular Biology paper on the TATA-binding protein bound to TAF1. At the LMB the work has stayed with mTOR and its relatives: a 2017 review with Williams on how TORC1 is activated by nutrients, a 2021 eLife study on how the inhibitor protein DEPTOR binds mTOR, and a 2024 review on the activation of PI3K-family enzymes. The Cambridge cancer centre lists Anandapadamanaban as an Investigator Scientist at the LMB.

highlights.ANA2019: First author: solved the cryo-EM and crystal structures of the human Rag GTPase pair alone and bound to mTORC1.

Anandapadamanaban M.note: Thesis year not shown on the page found; PhD dated only via Linkoping papers 2013-2015.

Berndt A.lab_name: Roger Williams group, MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (Cambridge, England, United Kingdom)
Berndt A.role: Protein scientist in Roger Williams' group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology who helped solve structures of PI3K enzymes and of mTOR and its partners
Berndt A.sub: Roger Williams group, MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge (papers 2010–2021; at the time of the studies)
story: Alex Berndt is a co-author of two structural papers in the Atlas from Roger Williams' group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology. The first (BAR2016) used cryo-electron microscopy on the Tor kinase bound to its partner Lst8. It showed that Tor pairs up into a dimer through a long, coiled stretch of helices at its front end, which helped explain how the much larger mTORC1 complex is built. The second (ANA2019) solved structures of the human Rag GTPases, the switch proteins that dock mTORC1 on the lysosome when amino acids are present, and showed how they bind mTORC1.

Berndt's work in the Williams group goes back to 2010, when Berndt was first author of a Nature Chemical Biology paper on the structure of p110delta, a PI3K enzyme important in immune cells, which showed how new inhibitors fit into it. PI3K and mTOR are related kinases with similar active sites. Berndt also contributed to a 2011 paper on how PI3K enzymes are switched on at membranes and to a 2021 eLife study on how the inhibitor protein DEPTOR binds mTOR.
No current institutional page could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas papers.

highlights.BAR2016: Co-author of the cryo-EM study showing that Tor forms a dimer through a long helical region at its N-terminus.
highlights.ANA2019: Co-author of the structural study of the human Rag GTPases and their complex with mTORC1.

Johnson CM.lab_name: Biophysics Facility, MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (Cambridge, England, United Kingdom)
Johnson CM.role: Biophysicist who built and ran the Biophysics Facility at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, measuring how proteins fold, bind and change shape for dozens of research groups
Johnson CM.sub: Head of the Biophysics Facility, MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge (2009–2022, semi-retired since) · MRC Centre for Protein Engineering, Cambridge (from 1992) · postdoc, University of Glasgow · PhD in protein folding, Department of Biochemistry at a Scottish university
story: Christopher Johnson is a co-author of two structural papers in the Atlas from Roger Williams' group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge. BAR2016 used cryo-electron microscopy to show that the Tor kinase, bound to its partner Lst8, pairs up into a dimer through a long coiled stretch of helices at its front end. ANA2019 solved structures of the human Rag GTPases, the switch proteins that bring mTORC1 to the lysosome when amino acids are present, and showed how they bind mTORC1. Pictures from microscopes and crystals are usually checked with solution measurements, for example of how tightly two proteins bind or whether a complex stays together in liquid, and that is the kind of work a biophysics facility provides.

Johnson studied biology, then did a PhD on protein folding in a biochemistry department in Scotland and a postdoc at the University of Glasgow on protein thermodynamics and calorimetry, the measurement of the heat released or absorbed when molecules bind. From 1992 he worked at the MRC Centre for Protein Engineering in Cambridge. When that centre closed he joined the LMB in 2009 as head of its new Biophysics Facility, which came to serve more than 50 research groups with calorimetry, spectroscopy and kinetic methods. He also built and adapted instruments with the LMB workshop.
In 2022 Stephen McLaughlin became head of the facility, and the LMB described Johnson as semi-retired and still supporting the team part-time with training.

highlights.BAR2016: Co-author of the cryo-EM study showing that Tor forms a dimer through a long helical region at its N-terminus.
highlights.ANA2019: Co-author of the structural study of the human Rag GTPases and their complex with mTORC1.

Johnson CM.note: Identity: very common surname. Ties are same institution and period (LMB 2016-2019), the middle initial M (talks.cam lists Dr Christopher M Johnson at LMB) and his facility role fitting a co-author slot on structural papers. His exact contribution to BAR2016/ANA2019 is not stated in any source seen, so the story does not claim it. Full name changed from 'Christopher Johnson' to 'Christopher M. Johnson'. LMB interview uses 'he'.

Baretic D.lab_name: Sir William Dunn School of Pathology, University of Oxford (Oxford, England, United Kingdom)
Baretic D.role: Structural biologist who, while at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, solved early cryo-EM structures of Tor and its relatives, and now works on ADP-ribosylation enzymes at Oxford
Baretic D.sub: Sir William Dunn School of Pathology, University of Oxford (papers since 2024) · MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge (Roger Williams group, then Joseph Yeeles group, papers 2014–2020)
story: mTOR is a huge protein, and for years nobody knew what its long front section looked like. Domagoj Baretić's 2016 paper in Nature Communications (BAR2016), from Roger Williams' group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge, used cryo-electron microscopy, a method that images frozen protein particles and combines thousands of pictures into a 3D model. Working with Tor bound to its partner protein Lst8, the team found that Tor pairs up into a dimer, and that its N-terminal region forms a long solenoid of stacked helices with an unusually complex fold. This helped explain the overall shape of mTORC1, which is also built as a dimer.

Baretić had earlier co-written a 2014 review with Williams on the structural basis of mTOR function, and in 2019 was first author of a review on the related DNA-damage sensors DNA-PKcs, ATM and ATR, which share mTOR's kinase design. A 2020 Molecular Cell paper, from Joseph Yeeles' group at the LMB, then showed by cryo-EM how the fork protection complex sits on the DNA replication machinery.

Since 2024 Baretić has published from the Sir William Dunn School of Pathology at the University of Oxford, in structural work with Ivan Ahel's and Marcin Suskiewicz's groups on enzymes that attach ADP-ribose to proteins. This includes a 2025 Nature Structural and Molecular Biology paper, as first author, on filament formation by the unusual human sirtuins FAM118, and contributions on PARP enzymes in the interferon response and in cancer drug action.

highlights.BAR2016: First author: solved the cryo-EM structure showing that Tor dimerizes through a long N-terminal helical solenoid.

Baretic D.note: Current position title at Oxford not confirmed by an official page; based on PubMed affiliations 2024-2026.

Gamblin SJ.lab_name: Scientific Platforms, The Francis Crick Institute (London, England, United Kingdom)
Gamblin SJ.role: Structural biologist and Fellow of the Royal Society who solved the crystal structure of active mammalian AMPK, the cell's energy sensor and the main counterweight to mTORC1, and who now directs the scientific platforms of the Francis Crick Institute
Gamblin SJ.sub: Director of Scientific Platforms, The Francis Crick Institute · Director of Science Operations, Crick (from 2015) · Director of Research (2011) and Joint Head of the Division of Molecular Structure (2005), MRC National Institute for Medical Research, Mill Hill · group leader, NIMR Division of Protein Structure (from 1994) · postdoc, Stephen Harrison lab, Harvard University · PhD in enzymology and crystallography with Herman Watson, University of Bristol
story: AMPK is the cell's fuel gauge. When energy runs low, the cell has more AMP and ADP (the spent forms of the energy carrier ATP), AMPK switches on, and one of the first things it does is put the brakes on mTORC1 so that the cell stops spending energy on growth. The 2011 Nature paper XIA2011, with Steven Gamblin as senior author, from his group at the MRC National Institute for Medical Research in London, showed how AMPK reads these signals. AMP binding to AMPK's regulatory gamma part protected the enzyme from losing the phosphate group that keeps it switched on. ADP binding to one site gave the same protection, though it did not directly activate the enzyme the way AMP does. The team also solved the crystal structure of an active AMPK complex, giving a 3D picture of how the energy-sensing part talks to the enzyme part.

The finding changed the textbook picture: ADP, which is far more plentiful than AMP in a stressed cell, can also keep AMPK on. That makes the energy brake on mTORC1 more sensitive than had been thought. The work was done with purified proteins and cells.

Gamblin studied biochemistry at the University of Bristol and did a PhD there with Herman Watson on enzymes and protein crystallography, followed by postdoctoral work in Stephen Harrison's lab at Harvard. In 1994 he set up his own lab in the new Division of Protein Structure at the National Institute for Medical Research, using structural biology to study proteins involved in disease. He became Joint Head of the Division of Molecular Structure in 2005 and the institute's Director of Research in 2011, the year he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society. When NIMR became part of the Francis Crick Institute he became its Director of Science Operations in 2015, and he is now Director of Scientific Platforms, overseeing the shared technology facilities. He is also a Fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences and a member of EMBO.

highlights.XIA2011: Senior author: showed that AMP and ADP protect AMPK from dephosphorylation and solved the crystal structure of an active AMPK complex.

Brohée L.lab_name: Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing (Cologne, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany)
Brohée L.role: Cell biologist who studied how lipid metabolism and the lysosome feed into mTORC1, first at the University of Liège and then at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing in Cologne
Brohée L.sub: Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing, Cologne, Cell Growth Control in Health and Age-related Disease group (papers 2021–2023; at the time of the studies) · Laboratory of Connective Tissues Biology, GIGA-Cancer, University of Liège, Belgium (papers 2015–2021)
story: Laura Brohée appears on two Atlas papers about brakes on mTORC1, the growth-control complex. The 2021 Cell study PRE2021 found that G3BP1 and G3BP2, proteins best known from stress granules, also sit on the outer surface of lysosomes and hold the TSC complex there. TSC is the brake that keeps mTORC1 in check, and without the G3BPs it could not reach its target, so mTORC1 over-reacted to amino acids and insulin. The 2023 Nature Cell Biology study NIC2023 found that malonyl-CoA, a building block made during fatty acid synthesis, fits into the same pocket of mTOR that normally binds ATP and blocks it. When fatty acid production slows and malonyl-CoA builds up, mTORC1 activity falls, which links the cell's fat-making capacity to its overall growth. Brohée was a co-author on the first and the second author on the second. Both were mainly cell studies; the 2021 paper added zebrafish experiments on nerve development.

Before Cologne, Brohée worked at the University of Liège in Belgium in the Laboratory of Connective Tissues Biology (Deroanne group), on cancer cell metabolism. As first author, Brohée showed in 2015 that the lipid enzyme lipin-1 shapes cancer cell behaviour and could make rapamycin treatment work better, and in 2018 that the heart drug propranolol made prostate cancer cells more sensitive to blocking glucose use. A 2021 review on lipin-1 as a cancer target followed.

At the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing, Brohée's papers list the Cell Growth Control in Health and Age-related Disease group, led by Constantinos Demetriades, which also produced a 2021 Molecular Cell paper on how TSC1 binds lysosomal lipids. No current institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas papers.

highlights.PRE2021: Co-author of the study showing that G3BP1 and G3BP2 tether the TSC complex to lysosomes and so restrain mTORC1.
highlights.NIC2023: Second author of the study showing that malonyl-CoA binds the mTOR catalytic pocket and acts as a natural ATP-competitive mTORC1 inhibitor.

Brohée L.note: NIC2023 has a 2026 Author Correction (PMID 42918817); not a retraction, only flagged for awareness. Deroanne named as group head only from last-author position (forename not given); 'University of Liège' spelled with diacritic.

Han JM.lab_name: College of Pharmacy, Yonsei University (Incheon, South Korea)
Han JM.role: Pharmacologist at Yonsei University who found that leucyl-tRNA synthetase, the enzyme that loads leucine onto its tRNA, doubles as the cell's leucine sensor for mTORC1, and who now studies how this enzyme links nutrients to growth signalling
Han JM.sub: College of Pharmacy and Department of Integrated OMICS for Biomedical Science, Yonsei University (papers since 2017) · Medicinal Bioconvergence Research Center, Seoul National University (Sunghoon Kim group, at the time of HAN2012)
story: Leucine is the amino acid that switches mTORC1 on most strongly, but in 2012 nobody knew which protein inside the cell actually detects it. Jung Min Han's 2012 Cell paper (HAN2012), from Sunghoon Kim's group at Seoul National University, proposed an answer. Leucyl-tRNA synthetase (LRS) is the enzyme that attaches leucine to its matching transfer RNA so the ribosome can use it to build proteins. The team showed in cultured cells that LRS also binds the Rag GTPases, the switch proteins that dock mTORC1 on the lysosome, and acts as a GAP for one of them in a leucine-dependent way. That turns the Rags to their active form and switches mTORC1 on. An enzyme everyone knew for its housekeeping job turned out to be a sensor as well.
The finding comes from cell experiments, and it gave the field a concrete candidate for the sensor that links leucine to mTORC1.

Han has kept working on LRS at Yonsei University, where Han is a faculty member in the College of Pharmacy and the Department of Integrated OMICS for Biomedical Science. As corresponding author, Han led a 2017 Nature Communications study showing that small molecules blocking the contact between LRS and the Rag protein RagD can dampen leucine-driven mTORC1 signalling, and later work on a pyrazolone-based inhibitor series built from that idea. Han also contributed to a 2019 Science paper showing that LRS1 controls leucine use depending on glucose supply, and was senior author on work showing that a sugar tag on LRS1 links leucine and glucose availability to mTORC1.

highlights.HAN2012: First author: showed in cells that leucyl-tRNA synthetase senses leucine and activates mTORC1 by acting on the Rag GTPases.

Han JM.note: No official Yonsei faculty page opened; position based on PubMed affiliations 2017-2022 with corresponding-author role. Exact academic rank not confirmed.

Schram AM.lab_name: Early Drug Development Service and Gynecologic Medical Oncology, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (New York, New York, USA)
Schram AM.role: Medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering who runs first-in-human cancer drug trials, including the first trial of RMC-5552, an mTORC1-selective inhibitor
Schram AM.sub: Associate Attending Physician, Gynecologic Medical Oncology and Early Drug Development, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center · fellowship in medical oncology, Memorial Sloan Kettering · residency in internal medicine, Brigham and Women's Hospital · MD, University of Pennsylvania
story: Rapamycin and the related rapalogs only partly block mTORC1, and the newer drugs that fully block mTOR also hit mTORC2, which causes high blood sugar and other side effects. RMC-5552 was designed to do better on both counts: it is a bi-steric drug that binds two sites on mTOR at once and is selective for mTORC1. Alison Schram was first author of the 2025 phase 1 trial in Clinical Cancer Research (SCH2025), the first time the drug was given to people. Fifty-seven patients with advanced solid tumours received rising weekly doses. Treatment-related high blood sugar occurred in only 4 percent of them and never limited the dose, and 64 percent had their disease controlled for a time.

These numbers fit the idea that sparing mTORC2 reduces metabolic side effects. The trial had no comparison group and did not test RMC-5552 against rapamycin or an older mTOR blocker, so it is early evidence and cannot show that sparing mTORC2 is the reason.

Schram studied medicine at the University of Pennsylvania, trained in internal medicine at Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston and in medical oncology at Memorial Sloan Kettering. At MSK the work centres on early-phase clinical trials that match new drugs to the molecular changes driving a patient's tumour, in the Early Drug Development Service and in gynecologic medical oncology, where Schram is an associate attending physician.

highlights.SCH2025: First author: reported the first-in-human dose-escalation trial of the mTORC1-selective inhibitor RMC-5552 in 57 patients with advanced solid tumours.

Roy A.role: Neuroscientist who studies brain inflammation in Parkinson's disease and now leads research on ME/CFS as Chief Scientific Officer of the nonprofit Simmaron Research
Roy A.sub: Chief Scientific Officer and Section Chief, Neurobiology, Simmaron Research · Adjunct Professor and member, Milwaukee Institute for Drug Discovery, University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee (since 2024) · Assistant Professor, Department of Neurobiology, Rush University Medical Center · PhD in neuroscience, Rush University Medical Center, Chicago
story: ME/CFS (myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome) is a long-lasting illness with severe fatigue that gets worse after effort, and it has no approved treatment. Avik Roy was senior author of a 2026 pilot study in the Journal of Translational Medicine (GIL2026) in which people with ME/CFS took low-dose rapamycin, the classic mTOR blocker. Fatigue went down. In blood plasma from the patients who responded, purine chemicals (building blocks of DNA and of energy carriers) shifted in a way that fits lower activity of the enzyme IMP dehydrogenase in their white blood cells. Lab experiments then suggested that altered purines can weaken mitochondria and push microglia, the brain's immune cells, into an inflammatory state.

The study was observational, without a placebo group, so it cannot show that rapamycin caused the improvement. The mitochondrial and microglial effects come from lab assays and were not measured in the patients.

Roy earned a PhD in neuroscience at Rush University Medical Center in Chicago and has been an assistant professor in its Department of Neurobiology. Much of the earlier work concerned glial activation and inflammation in Parkinson's disease, including the finding that loss of the gene for the protein BPOZ2 contributes to Lewy body pathology and the death of dopamine neurons, which won a Rapid Response Innovation Award from the Michael J. Fox Foundation. Roy is now Chief Scientific Officer and head of neurobiology at Simmaron Research, a nonprofit that studies ME/CFS, and since 2024 an adjunct professor and member of the Milwaukee Institute for Drug Discovery at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee.

highlights.GIL2026: Senior author: led the uncontrolled pilot linking low-dose rapamycin to lower fatigue and shifted purine metabolism in people with ME/CFS.

Roy A.note: Simmaron bio found on a squarespace mirror URL (appears to be Simmaron's own site). Rush profile lists Assistant Professor without dates; may be a past position.

Guerra P.lab_name: Molecular Systems Biology, Groningen Biomolecular Sciences and Biotechnology Institute, University of Groningen (Groningen, Netherlands)
Guerra P.role: Systems biologist who tracked TORC1 and PKA signalling in single yeast cells and showed that their growth signals rise and fall with the cell cycle
Guerra P.sub: PhD, University of Groningen (2022, thesis on single-cell analysis of TORC1 and PKA signalling during the budding yeast cell cycle; Andreas Milias-Argeitis group; at the time of the study)
story: Textbook diagrams show TORC1 (the yeast version of mTORC1) as a switch that is either on, when food is plentiful, or off, when it is not. Paolo Guerra's 2022 paper in the Journal of Cell Science (GUE2022), from Andreas Milias-Argeitis' group at the University of Groningen, looked at single cells instead of averages. Using time-lapse microscopy on hundreds of budding yeast cells, the team followed where two target proteins of TORC1 and of PKA (another nutrient-sensing kinase) sat inside the cell, which shows how active the kinases are. Their activity towards ribosome building rose and fell in step with the cell cycle, even though the food supply stayed the same the whole time. Mutations in regulators upstream of TORC1 and PKA changed the rhythm, which suggests that signals from the cell's own metabolism drive part of it.
For mTOR research this means that growth signalling is not only a reaction to the outside world but also has its own internal timing tied to cell division. The work was done in yeast.

The paper was part of Guerra's 2022 doctoral thesis at the University of Groningen, on single-cell analysis of TORC1 and PKA signalling and how growth and division are coordinated. In the same period Guerra contributed to a neural-network tool that outlines yeast cells in microscope images without hand-labelled training data, and to a 2022 study on what sets the timing of the Start checkpoint that commits a yeast cell to divide. No later position could be confirmed.

highlights.GUE2022: First author: showed by single-cell time-lapse imaging that TORC1 and PKA activity towards ribosome biogenesis oscillates with the yeast cell cycle.

Guerra P.note: Thesis supervisor not shown on the page seen; Milias-Argeitis named as group leader from last-author position on GUE2022 and the Groningen research page in search results. Current position not found.

Shackelford DB.lab_name: Shackelford Lab, Division of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine, David Geffen School of Medicine, University of California, Los Angeles (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Shackelford DB.role: Cancer biologist at UCLA who studies lung tumours that have lost the LKB1 tumour suppressor, the upstream activator of AMPK, and who trained in Reuben Shaw's lab at the Salk Institute
Shackelford DB.sub: Associate Professor, Division of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine, David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, and member, Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center · Molecular and Cell Biology Laboratory, Salk Institute for Biological Studies (Reuben Shaw lab, papers 2008–2013)
story: David Shackelford is a co-author of two Atlas papers from Reuben Shaw's lab at the Salk Institute that explain how AMPK, the cell's energy sensor, controls growth and recycling. GWI2008 found a second way AMPK shuts mTORC1 down. Besides activating the TSC2 brake, AMPK directly adds a phosphate group to Raptor, a core part of mTORC1, and this halts growth when energy runs low. EGA2010 showed that AMPK also adds phosphate groups to ULK1, the kinase that starts autophagy, which links low energy to the clearing of damaged mitochondria. Together the two papers describe a metabolic checkpoint: when fuel is short, the cell stops building and starts recycling.

The enzyme upstream of AMPK is LKB1, a tumour suppressor that is lost in many lung cancers. Shackelford's own work has followed that thread. A 2013 Cancer Cell paper from the Shaw lab, with Shackelford as first author, showed in mice that lung tumours lacking LKB1 respond to phenformin, a stronger relative of the diabetes drug metformin, because they cannot cope with the energy stress it causes.

At UCLA, Shackelford is an associate professor in pulmonary and critical care medicine. The lab uses genetically engineered mouse models of non-small cell lung cancer to study signalling and metabolism in tumours with KRAS and LKB1 mutations, tests compounds that selectively kill such tumours, and works on why LKB1-deficient tumours resist immune therapy. The American Lung Association has funded the lab through a Lung Cancer Discovery Award.

highlights.GWI2008: Co-author of the study showing that AMPK directly phosphorylates Raptor to switch off mTORC1 when energy is low.
highlights.EGA2010: Co-author of the study showing that AMPK phosphorylates ULK1 to link energy sensing to autophagy and mitophagy.

Shackelford DB.note: PMID 23352126 verified: first author, Salk affiliation with a UCLA e-mail, which ties the Salk and UCLA records. PhD and exact postdoc years not found.

Shah OJ.lab_name: Molecular and Cell Biology Laboratory, Salk Institute for Biological Studies (La Jolla, California, USA)
Shah OJ.role: Cell biologist in Tony Hunter's lab at the Salk Institute who showed that runaway Rheb-mTOR-S6K signalling destroys the insulin receptor's helper proteins IRS1 and IRS2, one half of the discovery of the S6K-IRS feedback loop
Shah OJ.sub: Molecular and Cell Biology Laboratory, Salk Institute for Biological Studies (Tony Hunter lab, at the time of the study)
story: When insulin binds its receptor, the signal passes through helper proteins called IRS1 and IRS2 before it reaches Akt and, further down, mTORC1 and its target S6K. O. Jameel Shah's 2004 paper in Current Biology (SHA2004), from Tony Hunter's lab at the Salk Institute, showed what happens when the end of that chain is stuck on. In cultured mammalian cells lacking the TSC brake, constant activity of Rheb, mTOR and S6K led to the loss of IRS1 and IRS2. The cells became resistant to insulin and their survival signalling through Akt weakened.

The paper appeared two months after a companion study by Harrington and colleagues, and together they set out the S6K-to-IRS negative feedback loop. In this loop, an overactive mTORC1 pathway turns down the very insulin signal that feeds it. The work was done in cultured cells.

PubMed lists Shah at the Salk Institute at the time of the study. Because PubMed also indexes an unrelated surgeon with the same initials, a full publication record could not be built safely, and no current position could be confirmed.

highlights.SHA2004: First author: showed in cultured cells that constitutive Rheb/mTOR/S6K signalling depletes IRS1 and IRS2, causing insulin resistance and weaker survival signalling.

Shah OJ.note: Patent records (TREA) list an Omar Jameel Shah of Lake Villa, Illinois as inventor on Abbott/AbbVie cancer combination-therapy patents (2010, 2014). Likely the same person (distinctive name, cancer signalling field) but no source ties him to the Salk paper, so it is left out of the text.

Belousova E.lab_name: Department of Psychoneurology and Epileptology, Moscow Research Institute of Pediatrics and Pediatric Surgery (Moscow, Russia)
Belousova E.role: Child neurologist and epilepsy specialist in Moscow who heads a department of psychoneurology and epileptology and has been a principal investigator in international drug trials for tuberous sclerosis complex
Belousova E.sub: Head, Department of Psychoneurology and Epileptology, Moscow Research Institute of Pediatrics and Pediatric Surgery (since 2003; at the institute since 1985) · Professor (2007) · Doctor of Medical Sciences (2004) · residency in child neurology, Leningrad · MD, Leningrad Pediatric Medical Institute (1980)
story: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a genetic disease in which a faulty TSC1 or TSC2 gene leaves mTOR permanently switched on. Children and adults with TSC grow benign tumours in many organs, including the brain and the kidneys, and most have epilepsy. Elena Belousova is a co-author of both large phase 3 trials of everolimus, a drug that blocks mTORC1, in this disease. In EXIST-1 (FRA2013), 117 patients with brain tumours called subependymal giant cell astrocytomas took everolimus or placebo; the tumours shrank by at least half in 35 percent of patients on the drug and in none on placebo. In EXIST-2 (BIS2013), 118 patients with kidney tumours called angiomyolipomas took part; 42 percent on everolimus had a response, against none on placebo.

These were randomised, placebo-controlled trials in people, and they are among the clearest evidence that blocking mTOR works when a genetic fault is the cause of mTOR overactivity. That does not mean the same benefit applies to people without such a mutation.

Belousova trained in medicine at the Leningrad Pediatric Medical Institute, graduating in 1980, and completed a residency in child neurology in Leningrad. She has worked since 1985 at the Moscow Research Institute of Pediatrics and Pediatric Surgery and has headed its Department of Psychoneurology and Epileptology since 2003. Her doctoral thesis (2004) was on seizures and epilepsy in children with cerebral palsy, and she became a professor in 2007. Her work covers the diagnosis and treatment of childhood epilepsy, and she has been a principal investigator in international trials in tuberous sclerosis and in Duchenne muscular dystrophy. She was named Honored Physician of the Russian Federation in 2011.

highlights.BIS2013: Co-author of EXIST-2, the phase 3 trial in which everolimus shrank TSC-related kidney angiomyolipomas in 42 percent of patients versus none on placebo.
highlights.FRA2013: Co-author of EXIST-1, the phase 3 trial in which everolimus shrank TSC-related brain tumours in 35 percent of patients versus none on placebo.

Belousova E.note: Full name updated to 'Elena D. Belousova' per journal editorial-board bio. Institute name on that page: 'Moscow Scientific Research Institute of Pediatrics and Child Surgery'; lab_name uses the PubMed English form. The bio page uses 'she'.

Whittemore VH.lab_name: Channels, Synapses and Circuits Cluster, Division of Neuroscience, National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, National Institutes of Health (Bethesda, Maryland, USA)
Whittemore VH.role: Neuroscientist and NIH program director for epilepsy and ME/CFS research who spent over two decades working for patient organisations, including the Tuberous Sclerosis Alliance
Whittemore VH.sub: Program Director, Channels, Synapses and Circuits Cluster, Division of Neuroscience, NINDS (since 2011) · ME/CFS research portfolio, NIH (since 2013) · nonprofit leadership, Tuberous Sclerosis Alliance, Genetic Alliance, CURE Epilepsy and NCHPEG (23 years) · faculty, The Miami Project to Cure Paralysis, University of Miami School of Medicine · postdoc, University of California, Irvine, and Fogarty Fellow, Karolinska Institute · PhD in anatomy, University of Minnesota Medical School
story: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a genetic disease in which mTOR is stuck on, so benign tumours grow in the brain, kidneys and other organs. Vicky Whittemore is a co-author of EXIST-1 (FRA2013), the phase 3 randomised trial of everolimus, a drug that blocks mTORC1, in 117 people with TSC-related brain tumours called subependymal giant cell astrocytomas. The tumours shrank by at least half in 35 percent of patients on everolimus and in none on placebo. The trial helped make everolimus a standard treatment for these tumours, and it is some of the cleanest evidence in people that blocking mTOR helps when a genetic fault drives it.

Whittemore trained as a neuroscientist: a PhD in anatomy at the University of Minnesota Medical School, postdoctoral work at the University of California, Irvine, and a Fogarty Fellowship at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, followed by a faculty position at the Miami Project to Cure Paralysis at the University of Miami. After her nephew was diagnosed with TSC she moved to patient-led research organisations and spent 23 years in that world, including at the Tuberous Sclerosis Alliance, the Genetic Alliance and CURE Epilepsy.

In August 2011 Whittemore joined the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke as a program director. She oversees grants on the basic mechanisms and genetic causes of epilepsy, including sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, and has also overseen the NIH research portfolio on ME/CFS since 2013.

highlights.FRA2013: Co-author of EXIST-1, the phase 3 trial in which everolimus shrank TSC-related brain tumours in 35 percent of patients versus none on placebo.

Whittemore VH.note: Full name changed to 'Vicky Holets Whittemore' (CURE Epilepsy URL slug and NINDS archive); revert to 'Vicky H. Whittemore' if preferred. Sources use 'she'.

Romashkan SV.lab_name: Division of Geriatrics and Clinical Gerontology, National Institute on Aging, National Institutes of Health (Bethesda, Maryland, USA)
Romashkan SV.role: Physician scientist at the National Institute on Aging who oversees clinical trials in older adults and led the safety analysis of CALERIE, the first long-term trial of calorie restriction in healthy people
Romashkan SV.sub: Division of Geriatrics and Clinical Gerontology, National Institute on Aging (papers 2006–2021; most recent confirmed affiliation 2021)
story: Cutting calories without malnutrition lengthens life in many lab animals, partly by turning down mTOR signalling. CALERIE was the first multicentre trial to ask what two years of calorie restriction does to healthy people who are not obese. Sergei Romashkan was first author of its safety report, ROM2016 in Oncotarget. Participants were assigned at random, two to one, to cut their intake by 25 percent or to eat as usual. There were no deaths and only one serious adverse event in the restriction group, and three people were withdrawn from restriction for safety reasons. Overall, side effects were not more common than in the control group. Bone mineral density at the spine and hip, however, fell more in the restriction group at 12 and 24 months, and the authors advised close monitoring for bone loss and anaemia.

For anyone thinking about calorie restriction, or about drugs meant to mimic it, the trial shows that the approach can be done safely under supervision but is not free of cost to the skeleton. It measured safety in people and did not test mTOR activity directly.

Romashkan works in the Division of Geriatrics and Clinical Gerontology of the National Institute on Aging, where the role centres on large clinical trials in older adults. Romashkan is a co-author of the design paper of the Testosterone Trials, seven coordinated trials of testosterone treatment in older men, and of the pilot of the LIFE physical activity trial. In 2021 Romashkan was first author of a report from an NIA workshop on how to test existing drugs and supplements for senolytic or senomorphic effects, meaning that they remove or quiet senescent cells, in clinical trials.

highlights.ROM2016: First author: reported that two years of 25 percent calorie restriction in non-obese adults was safe overall but lowered bone mineral density more than in controls.

Romashkan SV.note: No official NIA staff page found (web search budget ran out); current position not confirmed beyond the 2021 paper.

Wang Zhenhai.lab_name: Neurology Center, General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University (Yinchuan, Ningxia, China)
Wang Zhenhai.role: Neurologist in Yinchuan who leads cell studies of microglia, the brain's immune cells, and of how Brucella bacteria survive inside them
Wang Zhenhai.sub: Neurology Center and Diagnosis and Treatment Engineering Technology Research Center of Nervous System Diseases of Ningxia, General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University (papers 2011–2026)
story: Brucellosis is an infection passed from farm animals to people, and it can reach the brain. The bacteria survive inside immune cells instead of being destroyed. Zhenhai Wang was senior author of LI2026B, a 2026 paper in the Journal of Medical Microbiology that asked how a Brucella strain does this in microglia, the immune cells of the brain. The team used BV2 cells, a mouse microglia cell line, infected with Brucella suis vaccine strain 2. The bacteria pushed the cells into a mixed state between M1 (the inflammatory, bacteria-killing mode) and M2 (the calmer, repair mode) and switched on autophagy. The M2 state and autophagy together helped the bacteria multiply inside the cells, and the effect ran through the PI3K-Akt-mTOR pathway.

Normally, autophagy helps immune cells destroy invading microbes. This study suggests that some bacteria can turn it to their own advantage, with mTOR signalling as part of the switch. It was done in a cell line, so it shows a possible mechanism and not what happens in infected patients.

Wang works in neurology at the General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University in Yinchuan and in the hospital's engineering research centre for nervous system diseases. The group's PubMed record goes back to a 2011 study of how hepatitis C virus stimulates mouse microglia, and includes a cerebrospinal fluid research laboratory, BV2 cell lines engineered to lack particular phosphatases, a 2024 study on how exosomes from microglia affect myelin repair, and a 2025 study on how doxycycline kills human microglial cells infected with the same Brucella strain.

highlights.LI2026B: Senior author: led the cell study showing that Brucella suis vaccine strain 2 drives M2 polarisation and autophagy in microglia through PI3K/Akt/mTOR to favour its own replication.

Wang Zhenhai.note: Common surname: identity across papers rests on two ties (General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University and microglia/Brucella topic). No official hospital profile opened.

Demmings MD.lab_name: Neuroscience Program, Schulich School of Medicine and Dentistry, University of Western Ontario (London, Ontario, Canada)
Demmings MD.role: Neuroscience researcher in Sean Cregan's lab at Western University who showed that chronic ATF4 stress signalling shuts down mTOR and kills dopamine neurons in models of Parkinson's disease
Demmings MD.sub: Neuroscience Program, Schulich School of Medicine and Dentistry, and Robarts Research Institute, University of Western Ontario (Sean Cregan lab, papers 2020–2026)
story: In Parkinson's disease the dopamine-making neurons of the midbrain die. Matthew Demmings' 2026 paper in Cell Reports (DEMMINGS2026), from Sean Cregan's lab at Western University in Canada, traced one route to that death. In cell and animal models of the disease, a long-lasting stress response called the integrated stress response kept the transcription factor ATF4 active. ATF4 turned up three genes, SESN2, DDIT4 and TRIB3, whose proteins together lowered the activity of both mTOR complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2. That sustained loss of mTOR signalling switched on PUMA, a protein that triggers cell suicide, and the neurons died.

Much of the ageing literature treats lower mTOR activity as good. This study is a reminder that neurons need some mTOR signalling to survive, and that chronic shutdown can be harmful. The results come from cell and animal models, not from patients.

The paper builds on Demmings' earlier first-author study from the same lab, published in Cell Death and Differentiation in 2020, which showed that ATF4 promotes the death of neurons exposed to Parkinson's toxins and to clumps of the protein alpha-synuclein. In 2025 Demmings was also first author of a review on how neurons and glial cells interact from brain development to disease, and a co-author of a review on metabolic networks in the healthy brain.

highlights.DEMMINGS2026: First author: showed that chronic ATF4 signalling suppresses mTORC1 and mTORC2 through SESN2, DDIT4 and TRIB3 and drives PUMA-dependent death of dopamine neurons in Parkinson's models.

Demmings MD.note: Degree stage (PhD student vs postdoc) not confirmed; web search budget ran out before a lab page could be checked.

Correia-Melo C.lab_name: Leibniz Institute on Aging, Fritz Lipmann Institute (Jena, Thuringia, Germany)
Correia-Melo C.role: Ageing biologist who showed with João Passos in Newcastle that rapamycin can improve healthspan in mice without lowering inflammation, and later studied metabolite sharing between cells in Markus Ralser's lab
Correia-Melo C.sub: Leibniz Institute on Aging, Fritz Lipmann Institute, Jena (paper 2025) · Molecular Biology of Metabolism Laboratory, The Francis Crick Institute, London (Markus Ralser lab, papers 2019–2023) · PhD, Newcastle University Institute for Ageing and GABBA Program, University of Porto (papers 2016–2018)
story: Rapamycin extends life in mice, and a popular explanation is that it calms inflammaging, the low-grade inflammation that builds up with age. Clara Correia-Melo's 2018 paper in Aging Cell (COR2018), from João Passos' group at Newcastle University, tested this in mice lacking the gene nfkb1. These mice have overactive NF-kB, a master switch of inflammation, and they age early. Rapamycin did not lengthen their lives and did not lower their inflammation. It did make them less frail, improved long-term memory, coordination and the structure of several tissues, and lowered markers of senescent cells, which are cells that have stopped dividing and send out harmful signals.

The result separates two effects of rapamycin that are usually assumed to go together: in these mice the healthspan benefit happened without any drop in inflammation. The outcome was mixed, with positive healthspan results and null results for lifespan and inflammaging.

Correia-Melo did doctoral research at the Newcastle University Institute for Ageing through the GABBA graduate program of the University of Porto. As first author of a 2016 EMBO Journal paper with Passos, Correia-Melo showed that mitochondria are needed for many pro-ageing features of senescent cells. Postdoctoral work followed in Markus Ralser's Molecular Biology of Metabolism Laboratory at the Francis Crick Institute in London, where Correia-Melo was first author of a 2023 Cell paper showing that yeast cells that share metabolites with each other create a pro-survival environment that extends lifespan, and contributed to proteomic studies of COVID-19. In 2025 Correia-Melo was listed at the Leibniz Institute on Aging in Jena on a Science paper about protein translation in the ageing killifish brain.

highlights.COR2018: First author: showed that rapamycin improved healthspan in nfkb1 knockout mice without extending lifespan or reducing inflammaging.

Correia-Melo C.note: PhD details inferred from the 2016 EMBO J affiliation (Newcastle plus GABBA Porto); not confirmed by a thesis record. Current Jena role (postdoc or group leader) unknown. 'Jena, Thuringia, Germany' is a new location string.

Glass DJ.role: Muscle biologist in drug discovery, formerly at the Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research, who co-authored the first trials testing whether brief, low-dose mTOR inhibition can strengthen the ageing immune system
Glass DJ.sub: Regeneron Pharmaceuticals, Tarrytown, New York (papers since 2022) · Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research, Cambridge, Massachusetts (papers to 2019)
story: David Glass is a co-author of two Atlas trials from the Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research that asked whether a short course of a low-dose mTOR inhibitor can help the ageing immune system. In MAN2014, older volunteers took everolimus (RAD001), a rapamycin-like drug, for six weeks before a flu shot, and their antibody response to the vaccine rose by about 20 percent; fewer of their T cells carried PD-1, a marker of exhausted immune cells. In MAN2018, a phase 2a trial in 264 older adults, six weeks of a low-dose combination of everolimus and BEZ235 (a drug that blocks PI3K and mTOR at the active site) was linked to fewer reported infections over the following year.

These trials are the main human basis for the idea of weekly low-dose rapalogs as an anti-ageing intervention. Their limits matter: a stronger vaccine response is a lab marker, not proof of fewer infections, and a later phase 3 trial of BEZ235 (RTB101) alone did not confirm a clinical benefit.

Glass's own research line is skeletal muscle. At Novartis, as senior author, Glass led a 2019 study in aged rats showing that partial inhibition of mTORC1 with a rapalog counteracted the age-related loss of muscle mass, and contributed to work on how the enzyme HDAC4 keeps muscle in balance. Since moving to Regeneron Pharmaceuticals in Tarrytown, New York, Glass has published on how common low muscle mass is among people with obesity in the USA, on a 2025 trial identifying GDF8 (myostatin) and activin A as the main brakes on muscle mass in postmenopausal women, and in 2026 on why keeping muscle matters during drug-induced weight loss.

highlights.MAN2014: Co-author of the trial in which a short course of everolimus improved the flu-vaccine response of older volunteers by about 20 percent.
highlights.MAN2018: Co-author of the phase 2a trial in which low-dose BEZ235 plus everolimus was linked to fewer infections in older adults over the following year.

Glass DJ.note: Current employer from PubMed affiliations only (Regeneron 2022-2026); no official page opened (web search budget ran out). Two 2001 muscle papers in the Atlas list 'D J Glass' at Regeneron; the Regeneron and muscle ties make it likely they are the same person, but they remain uncounted here as before.
